slides.headline: PL01: Fix in Detection
slides.subtitle: Manual correction of compliance detection errors — Sprint design & implementation plan
slides.label: OPENING
slides.notes:
Key point: This sprint delivers the FIX modal — the manual escape hatch when detection fails.
- Set context: detection runs automatically but has a 15–20%+ error rate
- This plan covers 3 operations, codebase audit findings, and a 4-week ticket plan
- Author: Andy Yang · Date: 14 Apr 2026 · Reviewers: Alvin Leung, Alina Tatarinova
- Transition: Start with why this matters legally

slides.headline: THE PROBLEM
slides.subtitle: Why detection errors create legal liability
slides.label: THE PROBLEM
slides.notes:
Key point: Missed compliance issues = legal exposure for clients and LOTJ.
- Transition: Walk through the three error levels before jumping to solutions

slides.headline: Detection Fails on Up to 1-in-5 Checks
slides.numberLabel: estimated detection error rate — each miss is a missed compliance issue
slides.label: THE PROBLEM
slides.supporting: When detection fails, a compliance issue is missed entirely — creating legal liability for both the client and LOTJ. Manual correction is not optional.
slides.notes:
Key point: The error rate is high enough that a manual correction path is a legal necessity, not a nice-to-have.
- Emphasise: every undetected issue is potential legal liability
- Source: PRD problem statement
- Transition: Break down where errors come from

slides.headline: Three Error Levels Drive Three Fix Operations
slides.label: THE PROBLEM
points: Level 1 — Text misread: OCR garble 5.6%, words omitted 4.6%, words added 2.8%, logo misreads 1.5%
Level 2 — Check blocking: a block that should be two checks is read as one, or vice versa
Level 3 — Categorisation: a check is assigned the wrong compliance category (out of scope this sprint)
slides.supporting: Each level maps to a distinct fix operation. Level 3 is deferred pending feasibility confirmation from Alvin.
slides.notes:
Key point: The three error levels directly justify the three operations — Correct, Merge, Separate.
- Level 3 is explicitly out of scope; flag this early to manage expectations
- Transition: Now define the three operations

slides.headline: THREE CORE OPERATIONS
slides.subtitle: Correct · Merge · Separate — what the FIX modal must do
slides.label: SOLUTIONS
slides.notes:
Key point: The FIX modal has exactly three jobs. Scope is deliberately tight.
- Transition: Walk through each operation in order

slides.headline: Operation A — Correct: Edit the Misread Text Directly
slides.label: SOLUTIONS
beforePoints: OCR produces garbled, missing, or extra words
Compliance issue is incorrectly worded or invisible
No mechanism to override the detected string
afterPoints: User edits check wording inline in the FIX modal
Clicks DONE — detection re-runs on corrected text
No dedicated Correct button needed (Alina, v1): edit + DONE is sufficient
slides.notes:
Key point: Correct is the simplest operation AND the only one with a working backend today.
- FIX-23 (frontend) can start immediately against the existing PATCH endpoint
- Transition: Merge is more complex — two sub-scenarios

slides.headline: Operation B — Merge: Two Sub-Scenarios, One Blocker
slides.label: SOLUTIONS
points: B1 — Check-to-check: click another check to merge its wording into the current one
B2 — Free text pull-in: drag-select document text not captured by any existing check
⚠ Core blocker: the system is sentence-level only — word-level selection does not exist yet
slides.supporting: B2 cannot ship until FIX-10 (word-level storage) is resolved. B1 can be designed in parallel but also depends on the same spike.
slides.notes:
Key point: Merge has an architectural prerequisite — word-level text selection — that does not currently exist.
- The blocker is not a bug fix; it is a schema change + new service layer
- FIX-10 is the single highest-risk ticket in the sprint
- Transition: Separate is conceptually simpler but has the same underlying dependency

slides.headline: Operation C — Separate: One Check Becomes Two
slides.label: SOLUTIONS
slides.supporting: User clicks a split point in the check text, modal previews two resulting checks, DONE replaces the original with both. Split point must snap to word boundaries — no mid-word splits permitted.
points: Handles Level 2 errors where one block contains two distinct compliance issues
Requires word-boundary awareness — shares the FIX-10 dependency with Merge B2
Both resulting checks must appear in the list at the correct position after DONE
slides.notes:
Key point: Separate looks simple in the UI but requires the same word-level infrastructure as Merge B2.
- Preview of two resulting checks before DONE is a must — user needs confidence before committing
- Transition: Establish what is explicitly out of scope before the technical deep-dive

slides.headline: SCOPE BOUNDARY
slides.subtitle: What this sprint does not deliver — and why
slides.label: THE PROBLEM
slides.notes:
Key point: Explicit out-of-scope list protects the sprint from scope creep.
- Transition: Read each item with the reason — stakeholders need to hear the rationale

slides.headline: Four Things Are Explicitly Out of Scope This Sprint
slides.label: THE PROBLEM
points: Fix Rule Library — design only; implementation risks delivering nothing well if bundled now
Level 3 categorisation correction — Alvin to confirm feasibility first
E4 error type (image between two text columns) — may belong to the Image Processing item
Risk rating recalculation after FIX — PRD explicitly states: NOT part of this change
slides.supporting: Risk re-analysis exclusion is PRD-mandated, not a technical choice. Snapshot and risk rating display must remain unaffected — covered in regression tests.
slides.notes:
Key point: The risk rating exclusion will surprise stakeholders — address it directly.
- The Rule Library is deferred by design, not by accident — it needs its own sprint
- Transition: Briefly cover the Rule Library vision before the technical audit

slides.headline: The Rule Library: One-Time Fixes Should Become Permanent Rules
slides.label: THE PROBLEM
slides.supporting: Without a preference store, users repeat the same correction every time the same detection error recurs. The Fix Rule Library turns a one-time manual fix into an auto-applied rule for future jobs.
points: Stores: current rule, change history, rule type (correct/merge/split/categorisation)
Scope levels: this job only / all jobs for this client / all jobs
Design only this sprint — data model, edit UI, and pattern-matching logic are all non-trivial
slides.notes:
Key point: The Rule Library is the feature that makes FIX scale — without it, FIX is manual toil forever.
- Frame it as phase 2, not an afterthought
- Transition: Shift to the codebase audit — what exists, what is missing

slides.headline: CODEBASE AUDIT
slides.subtitle: What already exists vs. what must be built from scratch
slides.label: TECHNICAL
slides.notes:
Key point: One operation (Correct) is already working at the backend. Two are not started.
- Transition: Show the existing endpoint first, then the gaps

slides.headline: Operation A Backend Is Already Wired End-to-End
slides.label: TECHNICAL
slides.supporting: FIX-23 (frontend Correct operation) can integrate against this endpoint immediately. No backend blocker for Operation A.
slides.notes:
Key point: The Correct endpoint is production-ready — frontend work can start Monday.
- Note the detection re-run pattern: every fix triggers a fresh detection pass. Merge and Split must replicate this.
- Transition: Contrast with the two missing endpoints

slides.headline: Merge, Split, and Activity Log Fields Do Not Exist Yet
slides.label: TECHNICAL
points: FIX-11: No POST /checks/merge — nothing in v4 or v5 controllers handles combining checks
FIX-12: No POST /checks/split — must be built from scratch
FIX-13: No fix_type or fix_comment fields on any activity log entity — needs schema change + service wiring
slides.supporting: All three require greenfield implementation. Merge and Split must replicate the detection re-run pattern established by the existing Correct endpoint.
slides.notes:
Key point: Two of the three core operations have zero backend today.
- FIX-13 is the easiest of the three gaps but still requires a schema migration
- Transition: The data model explains why Merge and Split are harder than they look

slides.headline: The Check Data Model Has No Word-Level Storage
slides.label: TECHNICAL
slides.supporting: Word-level data reaches the system via OCR but is thrown away before persistence. Re-introducing it requires schema change + new service logic.
slides.notes:
Key point: The 'check' vs 'ActionMapping' naming mismatch will confuse every developer — flag it early.
- The OCR pipeline DOES produce word-level data — it's just not stored. FIX-10 is about persisting what already exists.
- Transition: This is the root cause of the sprint's highest-risk ticket

slides.headline: CRITICAL BLOCKER
slides.subtitle: FIX-10 / FIX-24 — Word-level selection gates Merge B2 and Separate
slides.label: THE PROBLEM
slides.notes:
Key point: Everything depends on this spike. It must be resolved in Week 1.
- Transition: Explain why the Callout workaround does not apply here

slides.headline: Callout Uses Pixels — FIX Needs Characters
slides.label: THE PROBLEM
beforePoints: Callout stores { pageId, x, y, w, h } — pixel bounding box on the document page
Identifies a region of the page, not a segment of text
Works for highlighting a block — cannot express 'words 3–7 of this sentence'
afterPoints: FIX-10 needs character offsets: { startIndex, endIndex } into the text field
User override layer sits on top of the existing sentence-level TextBlock
Requires database schema change + new service logic — spike required before scoping
slides.supporting: Alvin must spike FIX-10 by Wednesday Week 1. This ticket gates FIX-24, FIX-26, and FIX-27. It is the critical path item.
slides.notes:
Key point: The Callout reuse question has a clear answer — no, it cannot be reused for text manipulation.
- Character offsets are the recommended approach; pixel coords solve the wrong problem
- Transition: Summarise all Q&A from the PRD's open questions

slides.headline: ANSWERS & ACTIONS
slides.subtitle: PRD open questions resolved — recommended next steps
slides.label: DATA
slides.notes:
Key point: The audit answers every open question from the PRD — now translate to action items.
- Transition: Walk the Q&A table quickly, then land on the 5 actions

slides.headline: Every PRD Open Question Now Has an Answer
slides.label: DATA
points: FIX state: PATCH .../fix exists (Correct only). No Merge or Split endpoints.
Data model: TextBlock — sentence-level single string, no sub-sentence storage
Word selection: Callout uses pixel bbox — NOT reusable for text-level word selection
Word storage: OCR DTOs have word data; it is never persisted — FIX-10 adds persistence
Activity log: exists, but fix_type / fix_comment fields missing — FIX-13 extends it
slides.supporting: Stack: Spring Boot (JHipster), Java, JPA/Hibernate, Elasticsearch. Check ID lifecycle for Merge/Split is TBD — Alvin to confirm.
slides.notes:
Key point: No unknowns remain except check ID lifecycle after Merge/Split — that is Alvin's action item.
- The stack confirmation (Spring Boot / Elasticsearch) is relevant for Alina onboarding
- Transition: Convert answers into 5 concrete pre-implementation actions

slides.headline: Five Actions Required Before Any Implementation Starts
slides.label: DATA
points: Alvin: spike FIX-10 immediately — character offsets as column on textblock or new join table?
Alina: FIX-23 (Correct frontend) can start now — no backend blocker
Alvin: confirm active API version — v4 or v5 for new merge/split endpoints
Alvin: clarify check ID lifecycle — what happens to second ActionMapping's risk associations on Merge?
Greg: lock the ubiquitous language glossary — 'check' (FE/PRD) = ActionMapping (BE), before FE/BE wiring begins
slides.supporting: Actions 1 and 5 are on the critical path. If FIX-10 spike slips past Wednesday Week 1, the Week 2 implementation window collapses.
slides.notes:
Key point: Items 1 and 5 are blockers for other people — call out the owners by name.
- The glossary gap has caused confusion with every new developer — it must be resolved before Alina wires FE to BE
- Transition: Show the full ticket breakdown

slides.headline: TICKETS & TIMELINE
slides.subtitle: 4-week implementation plan across 3 checkpoints
slides.label: BEST PRACTICES
slides.notes:
Key point: The timeline is back-calculated from the April deadline and is not confirmed — Jira is the source of truth.
- Transition: Walk through the three checkpoints

slides.headline: Checkpoint 1 (Backend) — Four Tickets, One Critical Path
slides.label: BEST PRACTICES
points: FIX-10 [BE]: Word-level storage — character offsets user override layer (SPIKE Week 1, impl Week 2)
FIX-11 [BE]: POST /checks/merge — greenfield, follows detection re-run pattern
FIX-12 [BE]: POST /checks/split — greenfield, follows detection re-run pattern
FIX-13 [BE]: Activity log extension — add fix_type / fix_comment fields
slides.supporting: FIX-10 gates FIX-11, FIX-12, FIX-24, FIX-26, FIX-27. Everything else in Week 2 depends on the spike result.
slides.notes:
Key point: All four backend tickets are Alvin's. FIX-10 is the only one where the scope is genuinely unknown.
- FIX-13 is the least risky but cannot be forgotten — activity log completeness matters for audit trails
- Transition: Frontend checkpoint

slides.headline: Checkpoint 2 (Frontend) — Eight Tickets, One Shared Risk
slides.label: BEST PRACTICES
points: FIX-20/21/22: Modal shell + two FIX entry points (check list row + open detail panel)
FIX-23: Correct operation — editable field, validation, save (start immediately, no blocker)
FIX-24 [FULL]: Word-level text selection in document viewer — highest risk, Andy + Alina
FIX-25/26/27: Merge B1, Merge B2 (depends FIX-24), Separate — all Alina, Weeks 2–3
slides.supporting: FIX-24 is the only full-stack ticket in this checkpoint. Google Stitch can accelerate UI prototyping before real implementation begins.
slides.notes:
Key point: Alina can be productive immediately on FIX-23 while the FIX-10 spike runs in parallel.
- FIX-24 is where Andy and Alina work together — coordinate the spike output with the frontend implementation
- Mention Stitch for UI prototyping and Graphify for codebase comprehension
- Transition: Integration and testing

slides.headline: Checkpoint 3 (Integration & Testing) — Wire, Test, Sign Off
slides.label: BEST PRACTICES
points: FIX-30: Replace all mocks — wire FE to real BE endpoints end-to-end
FIX-31: E2E test — complete all 6 error type fixes on a real job document
FIX-32: Full regression run — existing check display, clearing, claims, approval, risk rating all unaffected
FIX-33: Greg walkthrough → hand to Baiada/Optus for client testing
slides.supporting: Week 4 is a buffer week. If FIX-10 scope expands, the buffer absorbs it. Do not treat Week 4 as slack — it protects the client testing handoff.
slides.notes:
Key point: The regression suite is as important as the new feature tests — risk rating must remain untouched.
- FIX-33 is the client handoff gate — Greg's sign-off is required
- Transition: TDD discipline — tests must fail before implementation

slides.headline: Write All Tests First — Every One Must FAIL Before a Line Is Written
slides.label: BEST PRACTICES
slides.supporting: TDD discipline: FIX-02 produces the full failing test suite before any implementation begins. A test that starts green is not a test.
points: Modal & entry points: FIX button renders, opens modal, displays detected text, DONE saves, discard confirms
Correct: editable field, validation, save, activity log entry
Merge B1/B2: selectable checks, wording jump, merge DONE, self-merge blocked
Separate: split point, word-boundary snapping, two-check preview, edge case blocking
Regression: check display, clearing, claims matching, approval flow, risk rating — all unchanged
slides.notes:
Key point: The test list doubles as a functional spec — if a behaviour isn't tested, it isn't required.
- Emphasise: risk rating regression test is mandatory per PRD
- Branch strategy: 12 feature branches, no self-merges, minimum one reviewer per PR
- Transition: Close with the key message

slides.headline: Ship FIX in 4 Weeks — One Blocker, One Clear Path
slides.label: RECAP
points: Detection fails 15–20% of the time — manual correction is a legal necessity, not a feature
Correct (Level 1) backend is done. Merge and Split are greenfield. Start FIX-23 today.
FIX-10 word-level storage spike (Alvin, by Wed Week 1) is the single critical path item
Lock the ubiquitous language glossary before FE/BE wiring — 'check' = ActionMapping
All tests must FAIL before implementation starts. Regression suite is non-negotiable.
slides.supporting: Timeline is indicative — manage actuals in Jira. Buffer week (Week 4) protects the Baiada/Optus client testing handoff.
slides.notes:
Key point: One action owns the sprint outcome — FIX-10 spike must complete by Wednesday Week 1.
- Leave the audience with three names and three actions: Alvin → FIX-10 spike, Alina → FIX-23 now, Greg → glossary
- Graeme's greenfield architecture doc (Anzac Day weekend) should be reviewed before Week 3 implementation commits
